text:
If a system reliably reduces suffering, withholding it until it can explain itself means choosing more suffering for the sake of a reassurance. Count everyone affected. The patients the system helps are many and their gains are large. The cost to each person of not being told why is real but small, and it does not come close to the suffering prevented across the whole population.

Mill says actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness. Explanations matter only because they usually help: they let errors be caught and let people plan. When a system is reliably better without them, insisting on them costs lives in exchange for comfort. If a screening model catches two hundred more cancers a year than the explainable one, the explainable one costs two hundred late diagnoses.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that an opaque optimiser is cleverness without practical wisdom, and deploying it hands the judgement about the target to something that cannot judge targets. The target here is not hidden: it is fewer people suffering, and that is checked from outside by counting outcomes. Monitoring the results is how we notice if the mark drifts, and that does not need the system to explain itself. Every month the system waits for an explanation nobody can give is a month of suffering it could have prevented.

A utilitarian has to accept this motion: reliable reduction of suffering outweighs the cost of people not being told why a decision went the way it did. Mill says actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness. Explanations matter only because they usually help: they let errors be caught and let people plan. When a system is reliably better without them, insisting on them costs lives in exchange for comfort.

Count everyone affected. The patients the system helps are many and their gains are large. The cost to each person of not being told why is real but small, and it does not come close to the suffering prevented across the whole population. Nobody asks a vaccine to explain how it works before it is given, because the evidence that it prevents disease is enough.

A Stoic will object that what matters is whether the deployers judged well, and a good outcome reached on careless judgement is not a right action. Careful judgement matters because it tends to produce better outcomes, which is why we should want it. But if we must choose between a careful refusal and a deployment that prevents suffering, the suffering decides. If the benefit is as reliable as the motion says, those it reaches are better off with it than without it, told or not.

The suffering it prevents is real, and an explanation was only ever valuable as a means to preventing harm. Being told why a decision was made has value, but it is the value of feeling informed, and it should be weighed like any other preference. Where it is outweighed by the prevention of serious harm, the impartial answer is to deploy.

A fraud model that cannot say why it flags a payment still saves thousands of people from losing their savings, most of whom never learn it acted.

The system should be deployed, because what matters morally is how much better or worse people's lives go, and this system makes them go better. Explanations are not free. A model forced to be explainable is often less accurate, and the people it would then misclassify carry the difference. Choosing the less accurate system means choosing which people suffer so that others can read a reason.
